title: Sarvam AI's Saaras V4 Brings Speech Recognition to All 22 Indian Languages
excerpt: The Bengaluru startup's new speech-to-text model covers 22 Indian languages plus English from a single 3-billion-parameter system, and claims it beats much larger global models on Indian speech.
body:
• Sarvam AI's Saaras V4 is a speech-to-text model covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages plus global English in a single system, built around a 3-billion-parameter hybrid state-space language model trained from scratch.
  • It offers five output modes — transcription, translation, transliteration, verbatim output and code-mixed speech — with streaming latency under 150 milliseconds for live voice agents.
  • Sarvam says the model outperforms larger global systems on Indian-language benchmarks, including roughly half the word error rate of Deepgram Nova-3 and GPT-4o Transcribe on noisy audio — though those numbers are company-reported.
  • The release also includes Sarvam Vision 2.1, a document model that reads handwritten Indic text, forms and multi-page tables across 22 languages.

Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI has released Saaras V4, a speech-to-text model that covers all 22 scheduled Indian languages plus global English in a single system. The company pairs an audio encoder with a 3-billion-parameter hybrid state-space language model as the decoder, trained from scratch — a direct bid to own the voice layer of Indian artificial intelligence. The launch, covered by WION and Business Standard, was paired with Sarvam Vision 2.1, a document-intelligence model for Indic scripts.

What the models do

Speech recognition for Indian languages is harder than for English, and not just because of the number of languages. Speakers routinely switch between languages mid-sentence, accents vary sharply by region, and much real-world audio comes from noisy streets or low-quality phone lines. Saaras V4 is built for those conditions. Its five output modes — plain transcription, translation, transliteration, verbatim output, and a code-mixed mode for blended speech — remove the post-processing developers normally bolt on. Keyterm prompting lets developers feed the model a list of up to 50 names, product terms or acronyms it should expect, useful for brand names and jargon that trip up general-purpose models. Speaker diarization is available through the batch API, and streaming latency stays under 150 milliseconds, fast enough for live voice agents.

Sarvam reports a language-identification error rate of 5.22% across 22 languages and 2.9% across the top 10, measured on verified IndicVoices data, and a 16.03% word error rate in the keyword-prompting setting of its IndicContextEval benchmark. The model ships through Sarvam's API at Rs 30 per hour, with Python and Node.js SDKs and voice-agent integrations.

"Saaras V4 is state of the art across all 22 Indian languages. 10 of these languages have no commercial alternative today."

— Sarvam AI, on X, September 23, 2026

Context & background

Sarvam is one of the companies selected under India's IndiaAI Mission to build indigenous foundation models, and it describes its stack as "sovereign by design" — developed and operated entirely in India. Voice is the interface through which hundreds of millions of Indians will use AI: customer service lines, banking, agriculture advisories and government services all run through speech, and many users are more comfortable speaking their own language than typing in English. Documents are the other bottleneck. Land records, government forms, old newspapers and handwritten notes are full of Indian scripts that standard optical character recognition handles poorly. Sarvam Vision 2.1 is aimed at that gap — reading multi-page tables, extracting fields from forms, and reading handwritten Indic text with what the company says is lower hallucination and lower inference cost than its February release. Sarvam also published a 6,909-sample Indic OCR benchmark drawn from newspapers, brochures, textbooks and texts dating to 1800; Vision 2.1 scores 87.39% overall — about 97% for Konkani but only 54% for Santhali.

Impact & analysis

The benchmark claims deserve scrutiny. Most of the comparisons against larger global models come from Sarvam itself, and some rely on a benchmark the company created. Independent evaluation on real-world audio and documents will be the real test, and the Santhali result is an honest reminder that coverage of 22 languages does not mean equal quality across them. Still, the direction is clear: Indian-language AI is moving from demos to production-grade tools that are fast, affordable and built for how India actually talks and writes — and at Rs 30 per hour, Saaras V4 undercuts the global speech APIs it is positioned against.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the release signals where Indian AI talent is building: sovereign systems tuned for Indian languages, not just layers on American models. NRIs serving Indian customers get a cheaper, locally operated voice stack — and Indian engineers at Google, Meta and OpenAI get a home-grown reference point.

What's next

Watch for independent evaluations of Saaras V4 on real-world audio, which will determine whether the company-reported numbers hold. Self-hosting remains a gap — the model is API-only today, with self-hosting documentation still covering the older v3 on SageMaker. The broader race to watch is the IndiaAI Mission's foundation-model program, where Sarvam's specialised, language-first approach competes against bigger, general-purpose Indian models still in training.
